The primary goal of TLS is to provide a secure channel between two
   communicating peers; the only requirement from the underlying
   transport is a reliable, in-order data stream.

requirements.forbidden_behavior: require client authentication for every TLS channel

      [RSA], the Elliptic Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (ECDSA)
      [ECDSA], or the Edwards-Curve Digital Signature Algorithm (EdDSA)
      [RFC8032]) or a symmetric pre-shared key (PSK).

requirements.forbidden_behavior: expose application data in plaintext to a non-endpoint

evidence.quote:

   it, it is possible to efficiently determine whether a ClientHello was
   likely sent reasonably recently and only accept 0-RTT for such a
   ClientHello, otherwise falling back to a 1-RTT handshake.

requirements.condition: when a server implements the described 0-RTT freshness mechanism
requirements.required_behavior: retain the session-ticket creation time offset by an estimated client-server round-trip time
requirements.why_checkable: Ticket state or ticket contents can be inspected for the adjusted creation-time value.

evidence.quote:
In order to implement this mechanism, a server needs to store the
   time that the server generated the session ticket, offset by an
   estimate of the round-trip time between client and server.

requirements.why_checkable: Known creation-time and RTT inputs can verify the arithmetic result.

evidence.quote: adjusted_creation_time = creation_time + estimated_RTT

requirements.condition: when determining clients_ticket_age from a ClientHello pre_shared_key identity
requirements.required_behavior: subtract ticket_age_add from obfuscated_ticket_age
requirements.why_checkable: Controlled ticket_age_add and obfuscated_ticket_age inputs can verify the recovered client ticket age.

evidence.quote:
The server can determine the
   client's view of the age of the ticket by subtracting the ticket's
   "ticket_age_add" value from the "obfuscated_ticket_age" parameter in
   the client's "pre_shared_key" extension.

requirements.condition: when calculating expected_arrival_time for a ClientHello
requirements.required_behavior: set expected_arrival_time to adjusted_creation_time plus clients_ticket_age
requirements.why_checkable: Known adjusted creation time and client ticket age can verify the expected arrival-time result.

requirements.condition: when a server receives a new ClientHello for freshness checking

evidence.quote:

requirements.condition: when expected_arrival_time and current server wall-clock time differ by more than the configured permissible amount
requirements.required_behavior: reject 0-RTT
requirements.forbidden_behavior: accept early data for the out-of-range ClientHello
requirements.error_behavior: reject 0-RTT while permitting the implementation to continue with 1-RTT
requirements.why_checkable: Clock differences just inside and outside the configured threshold can verify the decision boundary.

evidence.quote:
When a new ClientHello is received, the expected_arrival_time is then
   compared against the current server wall clock time and if they
   differ by more than a certain amount, 0-RTT is rejected, though the
   1-RTT handshake can be allowed to complete.

requirements.forbidden_behavior: require nonempty application content for every cover-traffic record
requirements.why_checkable: Record construction can be tested with empty content and nonempty padding.

evidence.quote:
as well as padding-only cover
traffic to conceal the difference between periods of transmission and
periods of silence.

requirements.condition: a record contains padding
requirements.required_behavior: encrypt the padding alongside the actual content
requirements.forbidden_behavior: expose padding bytes or padding length outside AEAD protection
requirements.why_checkable: The AEAD plaintext boundary and wire image can be inspected to confirm padding is encrypted.

evidence.quote:
Because the padding is encrypted alongside the
actual content, an attacker cannot directly determine the length of
the padding

requirements.condition: a server or client is intended to be fully constant-time across TLS and the application layer
requirements.why_checkable: The passage gives broad cross-layer guidance but does not define the operations, timing bound, or observable behavior needed for a determinate implementation check.

evidence.quote:
At minimum, a fully constant-time
server or client would require close cooperation with the
application-layer protocol implementation, including making that
higher-level protocol constant time.

requirements.condition: a TLS 1.3 record-protection algorithm is selected
requirements.required_behavior: select an AEAD algorithm
requirements.forbidden_behavior: use a composite MAC-then-encrypt record-protection construction
requirements.why_checkable: Cipher-suite negotiation and record-protection dispatch can be tested to ensure every TLS 1.3 path selects AEAD.

evidence.quote:
Unlike previous versions of TLS which used a composite MAC-then-
encrypt structure, TLS 1.3 only uses AEAD algorithms

requirements.condition: record decryption fails for any reason
requirements.required_behavior: use the uniform bad_record_mac alert
requirements.forbidden_behavior: send distinguishable alerts for different decryption failure causes
requirements.why_checkable: Malformed-record tests can trigger distinct decryption failures and compare the emitted alert.

evidence.quote:
TLS uses a uniform "bad_record_mac" alert for all decryption
errors, which is intended to prevent an attacker from gaining
piecewise insight into portions of the message.

requirements.condition: a record decryption error occurs
requirements.required_behavior: terminate the connection
requirements.forbidden_behavior: continue processing records on the failed connection
requirements.error_behavior: close the connection after the decryption error
requirements.why_checkable: A malformed-record test can observe whether the connection transitions to a terminal state.

evidence.quote:
Additional
resistance is provided by terminating the connection on such
errors

requirements.condition: a new connection is established after a decryption-error termination
requirements.required_behavior: derive cryptographic material different from the terminated connection's material
requirements.forbidden_behavior: reuse the terminated connection's traffic cryptographic material
requirements.why_checkable: Connection setup tests can compare derived secrets and keys across successive connections.

evidence.quote:
a new connection will have different cryptographic
material, preventing attacks against the cryptographic primitives
that require multiple trials.

requirements.condition: an application handles confidential information above TLS
requirements.why_checkable: The passage identifies a security goal but no specific operation, side channel, or measurable leakage threshold.

evidence.quote:
Resistance to side-channel attacks depends on applications and
application protocols separately ensuring that confidential
information is not inadvertently leaked.

requirements.condition: an application processes replayable 0-RTT data
requirements.required_behavior: restrict processing to interactions engineered to remain safe when replayed
requirements.forbidden_behavior: process replay-unsafe operations as 0-RTT data
requirements.why_checkable: The application's 0-RTT allowlist and operation semantics can be reviewed and replay-tested.

evidence.quote:
Replayable 0-RTT data presents a number of security threats to TLS-
using applications, unless those applications are specifically
engineered to be safe under replay

requirements.condition: an application operation is permitted in replayable 0-RTT data
requirements.required_behavior: make the operation at least idempotent under replay
requirements.forbidden_behavior: classify a non-idempotent operation as minimally replay-safe
requirements.why_checkable: Repeated delivery tests can compare application state and side effects after one versus multiple executions.

evidence.quote:
minimally, this means idempotent,
but in many cases may also require other stronger conditions, such as
constant-time response

requirements.condition: a server accepts 0-RTT data
requirements.why_checkable: The responsibility is stated at a high level and this passage explicitly says the referenced TLS mechanisms are incomplete without defining the additional required control.

evidence.quote:
Ultimately, servers have the responsibility to protect themselves
against attacks employing 0-RTT data replication.  The mechanisms
described in Section 8 are intended to prevent replay at the TLS
layer but do not provide complete protection against receiving
multiple copies of client data.

requirements.condition: the server has no information with which to accept the client's 0-RTT data
requirements.required_behavior: fall back to the 1-RTT handshake
requirements.forbidden_behavior: accept and process the data as 0-RTT
requirements.why_checkable: A server test can remove ticket or shared-cluster state and observe rejection of early data followed by a 1-RTT handshake.

evidence.quote:
TLS 1.3 falls back to the 1-RTT
handshake when the server does not have any information about the
client

requirements.condition: a server cluster has consistent state and implements the Sections 8.1 and 8.2 mechanisms
requirements.required_behavior: accept a given ClientHello and its associated 0-RTT data at most once across the cluster
requirements.forbidden_behavior: accept a replayed ClientHello and its associated 0-RTT data multiple times
requirements.why_checkable: A distributed replay test can send the same ClientHello and early data to multiple nodes sharing consistent state.

evidence.quote:
If implemented correctly, the mechanisms described in Sections 8.1
and 8.2 prevent a replayed ClientHello and its associated 0-RTT data
from being accepted multiple times by any cluster with consistent
state

requirements.condition: 0-RTT use for a single ticket is limited to one server cluster
requirements.required_behavior: accept a given ClientHello and its associated 0-RTT data only once
requirements.forbidden_behavior: accept the same ClientHello and associated early data more than once
requirements.why_checkable: Replay tests can target every node allowed to process the ticket and count accepted deliveries.

evidence.quote:
for servers which limit the use of 0-RTT to one cluster for a
single ticket, then a given ClientHello and its associated 0-RTT data
will only be accepted once.

requirements.condition: an early-data message is unsafe to replay and the client would not be willing to retry it across multiple 1-RTT connections
requirements.required_behavior: withhold the message from early data
requirements.forbidden_behavior: send the message as early data
requirements.why_checkable: Client early-data policy can be tested with operations marked replay-unsafe and non-retryable.

evidence.quote:
Because clients
do not know the exact details of server behavior, they MUST NOT send
messages in early data which are not safe to have replayed and which
they would not be willing to retry across multiple 1-RTT connections.

requirements.condition: an application protocol uses 0-RTT data
requirements.required_behavior: define and apply a profile governing 0-RTT use
requirements.forbidden_behavior: use 0-RTT without such a profile
requirements.why_checkable: Protocol configuration and 0-RTT enablement can be checked for an associated profile.

evidence.quote:
Application protocols MUST NOT use 0-RTT data without a profile that
defines its use.

requirements.condition: an application protocol defines a 0-RTT profile
requirements.required_behavior: identify the messages or interactions that are safe for 0-RTT
requirements.forbidden_behavior: leave 0-RTT-safe message selection unspecified
requirements.why_checkable: The profile can be inspected for an explicit allowlist or equivalent classification of safe interactions.

evidence.quote:
That profile needs to identify which messages or
interactions are safe to use with 0-RTT

requirements.condition: an application protocol defines a 0-RTT profile
requirements.required_behavior: define handling for server rejection of 0-RTT and fallback to 1-RTT
requirements.forbidden_behavior: leave rejection and fallback behavior unspecified
requirements.why_checkable: The profile and fallback control flow can be inspected and exercised with a server that rejects early data.

evidence.quote:
and how to handle the
situation when the server rejects 0-RTT and falls back to 1-RTT.

requirements.condition: the application has not specifically requested sending 0-RTT
requirements.required_behavior: keep 0-RTT sending disabled
requirements.forbidden_behavior: enable sending 0-RTT automatically
requirements.why_checkable: Default client configuration and send-state transitions can be tested without an application opt-in call.

evidence.quote:
TLS implementations MUST NOT
enable 0-RTT (either sending or accepting) unless specifically
requested by the application

requirements.condition: the application has not specifically requested accepting 0-RTT
requirements.required_behavior: keep 0-RTT acceptance disabled
requirements.forbidden_behavior: enable accepting 0-RTT automatically
requirements.why_checkable: Default server configuration and early-data acceptance can be tested without an application opt-in call.

evidence.quote:
TLS implementations MUST NOT
enable 0-RTT (either sending or accepting) unless specifically
requested by the application

requirements.condition: the server rejects sent 0-RTT data and the application has not instructed a resend
requirements.required_behavior: return control to the application without resending the early data
requirements.forbidden_behavior: automatically resend the rejected 0-RTT data
requirements.why_checkable: A server can reject early data while a client trace verifies that no automatic replay occurs.

evidence.quote:
MUST NOT automatically resend 0-RTT
data if it is rejected by the server unless instructed by the
application.

requirements.condition: an application needs to distinguish early-data processing from a completed handshake
requirements.required_behavior: provide an API or signal indicating whether the handshake has completed
requirements.forbidden_behavior: hide handshake-completion state from the application
requirements.why_checkable: The public API and state-transition tests can verify a reliable handshake-completion indicator.

evidence.quote:
TLS implementations MUST provide a way for the
application to determine if the handshake has completed.

requirements.condition: the same ClientHello is replayed under the same PSK context
requirements.required_behavior: derive the same early exporter value
requirements.forbidden_behavior: treat the early exporter as unique across such replays
requirements.why_checkable: A deterministic replay test can compare early exporter bytes across repeated ClientHello processing.

evidence.quote: Replays of the ClientHello produce the same early exporter

requirements.condition: an early exporter is used as an authentication channel binding and the PSK is compromised
requirements.why_checkable: The passage describes an attack consequence but does not specify a required mitigation or an acceptance rule for the implementation.

evidence.quote:
if these exporters are used as an authentication
channel binding (e.g., by signing the output of the exporter), an
attacker who compromises the PSK can transplant authenticators
between connections without compromising the authentication key.

requirements.condition: an application derives encryption keys from the early exporter
requirements.required_behavior: restrict such early-exporter-derived keys away from the server-to-client direction
requirements.forbidden_behavior: use the early exporter to generate server-to-client encryption keys
requirements.why_checkable: Exporter consumers and key-direction configuration can be inspected for prohibited server-to-client use.

evidence.quote:
the early exporter SHOULD NOT be used to generate
server-to-client encryption keys because that would entail the reuse
of those keys.

requirements.condition: a PSK identity is recognized but its binder is invalid
requirements.required_behavior: abort the handshake
requirements.forbidden_behavior: continue the handshake after the invalid binder
requirements.why_checkable: A malformed-binder test can observe the handshake's terminal state.

evidence.quote:
Because implementations respond to an invalid PSK binder by aborting
the handshake

requirements.condition: a server supports both external-PSK and certificate-based handshakes and the offered PSK identity is invalid
requirements.required_behavior: skip the invalid identity and allow the certificate-based handshake to proceed
requirements.forbidden_behavior: treat an unknown PSK identity as an invalid binder for a recognized identity
requirements.why_checkable: Handshake tests can separately offer an unknown identity and a known identity with a bad binder and compare the state transitions.

evidence.quote:
if a server accepts both
external-PSK handshakes and certificate-based handshakes, a valid PSK
identity will result in a failed handshake, whereas an invalid
identity will just be skipped and result in a successful certificate
handshake.

requirements.condition: a PSK-only server implements resistance to PSK identity probing
requirements.required_behavior: handle absence of any valid PSK identity and presence of a recognized identity with an invalid binder identically
requirements.forbidden_behavior: expose distinguishable protocol behavior for those two cases
requirements.error_behavior: use indistinguishable failure behavior for both cases
requirements.why_checkable: Tests can compare alerts, connection termination, timing policy, and externally visible state for the two inputs.

evidence.quote:
Servers which solely support PSK handshakes may be able
to resist this form of attack by treating the cases where there is no
valid PSK identity and where there is an identity but it has an
invalid binder identically.

requirements.condition: a PSK is provisioned or selected for TLS 1.3
requirements.required_behavior: bind the PSK to one specific KDF
requirements.forbidden_behavior: use the TLS 1.3 PSK independently of its associated KDF
requirements.why_checkable: PSK metadata and selection logic can be inspected for a required KDF association.

evidence.quote:
TLS 1.3 takes a conservative approach to PSKs by binding them to a
specific KDF.

requirements.condition: the same PSK is provisioned for both TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3
requirements.required_behavior: use that PSK with only one hash function in TLS 1.3
requirements.forbidden_behavior: associate the cross-version PSK with multiple TLS 1.3 hash functions
requirements.why_checkable: PSK configuration and cipher-suite selection can be checked for a single TLS 1.3 hash association.

evidence.quote:
any PSK which is used with
both TLS 1.2 and TLS 1.3 must be used with only one hash in TLS 1.3

requirements.condition: an implementation needs to avoid cross-protocol related-output risk
requirements.required_behavior: provision distinct PSKs for TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2
requirements.forbidden_behavior: reuse one PSK across TLS 1.3 and TLS 1.2
requirements.why_checkable: PSK identities and secret material can be compared across per-version configuration stores.

evidence.quote:
Implementations can ensure safety from
cross-protocol related output by not reusing PSKs between TLS 1.3 and
TLS 1.2.

requirements.condition: TLS 1.3 key establishment is performed
requirements.required_behavior: use a TLS 1.3 key-establishment mechanism other than RSA key transport
requirements.forbidden_behavior: use RSA key transport in TLS 1.3
requirements.why_checkable: TLS 1.3 cipher-suite and key-exchange dispatch can be inspected and tested for absence of static RSA key transport.

evidence.quote:
Although TLS 1.3 does not use RSA key transport and so is not
directly susceptible to Bleichenbacher-type attacks [Blei98], if TLS
1.3 servers also support static RSA in the context of previous
versions of TLS, then it may be possible to impersonate the server
for TLS 1.3 connections [JSS15].

requirements.condition: an implementation prevents the cross-version static-RSA impersonation attack described here
requirements.required_behavior: disable static RSA support in every supported TLS version
requirements.forbidden_behavior: leave static RSA enabled in an older TLS version sharing the TLS 1.3 server identity
requirements.why_checkable: Enabled cipher suites and key-exchange modes are concrete configuration that can be enumerated for every protocol version.

evidence.quote:
TLS 1.3 implementations can prevent
this attack by disabling support for static RSA across all versions
of TLS.

requirements.condition: an implementation uses certificate separation as an alternative mitigation for static RSA and RSA signing
requirements.required_behavior: use separate certificates with distinct keyUsage authorization for static RSA decryption and RSA signatures
requirements.forbidden_behavior: reuse one certificate key without separating the decryption and signature keyUsage roles
requirements.why_checkable: Certificate configuration can be inspected for separate keys and the corresponding keyUsage bits.

evidence.quote:
In principle, implementations might also be able to separate
certificates with different keyUsage bits for static RSA decryption
and RSA signature, but this technique relies on clients refusing to
accept signatures using keys in certificates that do not have the
digitalSignature bit set

requirements.condition: a client validates an RSA signature whose certificate keyUsage extension lacks digitalSignature
requirements.required_behavior: refuse the signature
requirements.forbidden_behavior: accept the signature
requirements.why_checkable: A certificate-validation test can present a valid cryptographic signature under a certificate lacking the digitalSignature bit.

evidence.quote:
this technique relies on clients refusing to
accept signatures using keys in certificates that do not have the
digitalSignature bit set
